catalog_quote: Southeast Asian languages generally lack the alternating patterns of multiple stress levels which immediately lend themselves to analysis in terms of metrical feet. ... Following Hayes 1994, I take stress to be abstract, realized structurally on the head syllables of prosodic constituents. The exponents of stress in Thai and Kayah Li are two syllable weight and tonality, two binary oppositions (which accounts for the lack of multiple stress levels). The close association of syllable weight with foot headship, plus a consistent pattern of metrical right-headedness, derives iambic foot structure, and forms the basis for the frequent distinction between major syllables and minor syllables.

sweep_summary: Western Kayah (west2409) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title has one title-keyword item, Bennett 1995 (UIUC PhD, Thai + Kayah Li iambic foot structure). Its body remains inaccessible: IDEALS JSON API lists the file but both bitstreams could not be reached by automated download (UIUC NetID only); Google Books has a record (8R5FHQAACAAJ) without preview; Only the abstract was read: stress is abstract prominence on the head of a right-headed iambic foot, realized by syllable weight and tone, giving the major/minor syllable distinction; the Kayah Li dialect is not named, though Bryant 1996 (pp. 73, 88-89) cites Bennett's Chulalongkorn lab work on Western Kayah Li. The only first-hand Western Kayah Li phonology held by the project (Bryant 1996, Rosetta scans pp. 66-97) is silent on stress. A Crossref probe surfaced Kato 2021 (Karenic typological profile, De Gruyter, paywalled) as a low-priority secondary lead. No new first-hand stress statement was obtained; Bennett 1995 is the high-priority acquisition (ILL/ProQuest 9543532/Harvard the Harvard library catalogue).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Abstract-level only: Kayah Li has no audible multi-level stress; 'stress' is the head of a right-headed (iambic) foot, and foot headship coincides with syllable weight and full tone. In practice the full (major, tone-bearing) syllable is the head and the reduced minor/prefix syllable (Bryant's ta-, a-, i- presyllables) is the non-head, i.e. prominence falls on the major syllable that follows a minor syllable; monosyllables are their own foot. The body of the dissertation (with the actual rule and the dialect) could not be read.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Abstract says the language lacks 'the alternating patterns of multiple stress levels'; nothing further seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Abstract says 'phonologically distinct speech styles' (hyper- vs hypo-articulated) have different constraint rankings, i.e. foot structure/reduction varies by style.
new_statements.domain_note: Foot/word level (major + minor syllable sequences); the only accessible primary description of Western Kayah Li (Bryant 1996) is silent on stress altogether and gives only tone (4 tones), phonation and syllable-count facts.
new_statements.identity_note: Bryant 1996 describes the Kyebogyi dialect of Western Kayah Li (spoken west of the Pun/Salween rivers) from speakers resettled in Mae Hong Son, Thailand. Bennett 1995 says only 'Kayah Li'; Glottolog assigns it to kyu (west2409) and Bryant 1996 (pp. 73, 88-89) cites Bennett's Chulalongkorn phonetics-lab work on Western Kayah Li tone, so the data are at least partly Western. Solnit's grammar, the SEALS 1992 paper and the 2003 Routledge chapter (listed under west2409 by Glottolog) describe EASTERN Kayah Li (east2342, Lower/ke-ke dialect, Mae Hong Son); Bryant p. 91 reports the two are nearly mutually intelligible, differing in phonation.
